column1: # Aramaic for the "Write in ..." tool (scribe.js); built into scribe-langs.js by scripts/make-scribe.ps1.
# Two scripts with the same 22 letters: Imperial Aramaic, the chancery script of the Persian empire, and Syriac in its
# oldest book hand, Estrangela. rules=aramaic: short vowels inside a word are not written, i/ē and o/u become yodh and
# waw, a word-initial vowel takes aleph, and a final a takes aleph (the "emphatic" -ā of nouns: malkā, mlkʾ).

column4: Aramaic is written from right to left in 22 letters, all consonants, like Hebrew and Phoenician; its alphabet spread across the Persian empire and gave rise to the Hebrew, Syriac, Nabataean and Arabic scripts.

column2: The letters of the Persian chancery (6th–4th centuries BCE), used for letters and contracts from Egypt to Afghanistan, as in the papyri of Elephantine.

Type as it sounds: sh for š, ch for ḥ, ts for ṣ, ' for aleph and ` for ʿayin. Short vowels inside a word are left out; i becomes י-like yodh and o or u waw; a final a is written with aleph, as in malka, mlkʾ, “the king”.

column4: aleph · a catch in the throat; also a final a
waw · w; also o and u
ʿayin · a sound squeezed in the throat
qoph · k, said deep in the throat

column3: “Mene, mene, tekel, upharsin”: the writing on the wall at Belshazzar’s feast

column2: The script of Syriac, the Aramaic of Edessa and of the Christians of Mesopotamia, in Estrangela, its oldest book hand (from the 1st century CE); the letters join like Arabic.
The same 22 letters, joined in Syriac fashion. Type as for Imperial Aramaic: sh, ch, ts, ' for alaph and ` for ʿe. Short vowels inside a word are left out; a final a takes alaph, as in shlama, ܫܠܡܐ.

column4: alaph · a catch in the throat; also a final a
waw · w; also o and u
ʿe · a sound squeezed in the throat
qaph · k, said deep in the throat

column3: “Our Father, who art in heaven”: the Lord’s Prayer in the Syriac Bible
